```{r setup}
library(cancensus)
library(dplyr)
```

## Background
Attribute files describe the detailed relationship of various Statistics Canada geographic levels and provide population, household and dewlling counts. This information can be useful for understanding the hierarchical relationships of different geographic levels. The [CensusMapper API](https://censusmapper.ca/api) that **cancensus** uses for most of the data queries is ill-suited to get comprehensive data on the hierarichal relationships Canada wide, so it can be helpful to have direct access to this data in comprehensive tabular form.

## Match between Census Tracts and Census Subdivisions
If we are interested in understanding which Census Tracts respect municipal boundaries and which ones don't in 2021 we can consult the geographic attributes file. It contains a row for each Census Block, the basic building block of census geographies, and tags other levels of geography the Census Block lies in.

Statistics Canada blocks programmatic downloads of these files, so `get_statcan_geographic_attributes()` reads copies hosted as parquet files, which requires the **duckdb** and **DBI** packages. The result says where the data comes from.

```{r}
attributes <- get_statcan_geographic_attributes("2021")
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
# Skip the remaining chunks if the download failed, e.g. on CI
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = !is.null(attributes))
```

```{r}
attr(attributes, "metadata")$attribution_en
attr(attributes, "metadata")$licence_en
```

```{r}
attributes %>% colnames()
```

To answer our question, we filter Census Block by the ones that lie within a Census Tract, and check for the collection of Census Blocks within each Census Tract how many municipalities they lie in.

```{r}
attributes %>%
  filter(CMATYPE %in% c("B","K")) |> # filter areas not in CTs
  group_by(CTCODE,CMATYPE) |>
  summarise(`Number of municipalities`=length(unique(CSDUID)),.groups="drop") |>
  count(`Number of municipalities`,CMATYPE) |>
  arrange(CMATYPE,`Number of municipalities`)
```

This shows that most census tracts for both Census Metropolitan Areas (CMATYPE="B") and tracted Census Agglomerations (CMATYPE="K") lie within a single municipality, with some census tracts spanning several municipalities.

## Older censuses
Attribute files are available back to 1981. From 2001 on they have a row for each Census Block, identified by `DBUID`. Earlier censuses have a row for each Enumeration Area, identified by `EAUID`, and different columns. Each column has a description in its `"label"` attribute, and the metadata of each file has notes on how it was built and on problems with the source.

```{r}
attributes_1981 <- get_statcan_geographic_attributes("1981")
attributes_1981 %>% colnames()
attr(attributes_1981$EAPHH1981, "label")
attributes_1981 %>% summarise(Population = sum(EAPOP1981, na.rm = TRUE))
attr(attributes_1981, "metadata")$notes_en
```

## Representative points
The attribute files have representative points for each area, as latitude and longitude and in some years also as projected coordinates. The metadata of each coordinate column gives its coordinate reference system: the EPSG code in `crs_epsg` where there is one, the PROJ string in `crs_proj`, and in `crs_en` how this was established. In most years the source documentation doesn't state the datum, so it was inferred by checking the columns against each other, which `crs_basis` records.

```{r}
point_metadata <- attr(attributes, "metadata")$columns$DARPLAT
point_metadata$crs_en
point_metadata$crs_basis
```

From 2006 on the representative points belong to dissemination areas, and each point is repeated on every block row of its dissemination area. Converting the rows directly would stack all blocks of a dissemination area on one point, so we first reduce the data to one row per dissemination area, here for Metro Vancouver, before converting it to an **sf** object with the CRS from the metadata.

```{r}
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

da_points <- attributes %>%
  filter(CMAUID == "933") %>%
  group_by(DAUID, DARPLONG, DARPLAT) %>%
  summarise(Population = sum(DBPOP2021, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("DARPLONG", "DARPLAT"), crs = point_metadata$crs_epsg)

ggplot(da_points) +
  geom_sf(aes(size = Population), alpha = 0.3, shape = 16) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Metro Vancouver dissemination area representative points, 2021")
```

The points differ between census years:

* 2001 is the only year with block level points, in `DBRPLAT` and `DBRPLONG`, in addition to the dissemination area points.
* 1981 to 1996 have one point per enumeration area, but on the NAD27 datum (EPSG:4267) rather than NAD83. Transforming them to NAD83 is most accurate with the Canadian NTv2 grid, which PROJ can fetch when network access is enabled with `sf::sf_proj_network(TRUE)`. The projected Lambert columns of these years are on NAD27 as well and should not be read as EPSG:3347.
* 1981 and 1986 give latitude and longitude only to the whole minute, about 1.85 km north to south, so many enumeration areas share a point. The UTM columns are more precise, but their zone varies by row.

The `precision_en` entry of the column metadata has the details.

```{r}
attributes_1996 <- get_statcan_geographic_attributes("1996")
crs_1996 <- attr(attributes_1996, "metadata")$columns$EARPLAT$crs_epsg
crs_1996

ea_points <- attributes_1996 %>%
  filter(CMAUID == "933") %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("EARPLONG", "EARPLAT"), crs = crs_1996) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(da_points))
```
